content: 1. Begin by asking participants to describe their observations regarding the interactions between the caregiver and the child. 2. Inquire whether the caregiver demonstrated sensitivity to the child’s cues. 3. Assess the appropriateness of the caregiver’s responses to the child’s needs and behaviors. 4. Evaluate whether there was a visible connection or bond between the caregiver and the child. 5. Ask participants to reflect on what the counselor did to enhance the interactions between the caregiver and the child. 6. Discuss how these interactions might influence the child’s survival, development, and learning. 7. Add your own observations if necessary. 8. Ask caregivers how they encourage their child to smile. 9. Note that parents who frequently and effectively interact with their children often learn how to elicit smiles from their children, even at a very young age. 10. At the conclusion of the discussion, transition participants to the area where they will practice counseling caregivers. 11. Request facilitators to bring a caregiver and child to each pair of participants. 12. Observe the counseling sessions and listen to the feedback provided by facilitators to help participants improve their skills. 13. Take detailed notes on the counseling sessions to debrief participants on their experiences with caregivers and children. 14. After the counseling session, return to the classroom to conduct a debriefing. 15. Following a break, discuss four or five examples of caregiver-child interactions observed during the session, including: Positive interactions where the caregiver was attentive to the child and sensitive to their cues, and the child responded by looking at the caregiver. Negative interactions where there was minimal connection between the caregiver and the child, such as high activity with little engagement or low activity with minimal responsiveness. The responses of both the caregiver and the child to play and communication activities. Any changes in the interactions between caregivers and children during the activities. 16. On Day 3, discuss the challenges caregivers anticipated or experienced when playing and communicating with their children at home. 17. Explore how participants were able to assist caregivers in addressing these challenges. 18. Discuss what participants found easy to do and what they found difficult. 19. If available, use photos or videos from the session to illustrate key discussion points. 20. During clinical sessions, participants demonstrate their skills, allowing clinical instructors and facilitators to monitor their progress. 21. At the end of each day, facilitators meet to review the day’s activities and prepare for the next day. 22. The clinical instructor summarizes each participant’s progress during these meetings. 23. Facilitators discuss: How well participants are performing in both classroom and clinical settings. Any difficulties participants are encountering. Strategies to address these difficulties, such as: Assigning a facilitator to work closely with participants who are struggling, providing direct coaching in both classroom and clinical settings. Pairing stronger participants with weaker ones during clinical sessions. Reviewing skills in the classroom before the next clinical session. Improving the preparation and organization of clinical sessions to allow for more supervised practice. 24. During inpatient sessions, participants observe a demonstration lasting 15 minutes, which includes: Approaching a sick child. Gaining the child’s attention. Following the child’s lead by mimicking their sounds and gestures. Engaging in play and communication activities using age-appropriate toys and methods suitable for the child’s condition. Encouraging the child to increase their activity level and develop new skills. Praising the child for their efforts in learning new activities. 25. During grand rounds (30 minutes), counselors present two or three sample cases of children they worked with, discussing: How they approached the child. How they gained the child’s attention. How they followed the child’s lead. The play or communication activity chosen and the rationale behind it. The child’s response to the activity and what strategies were effective in engaging the child. Changes in the child’s activity level and what the child learned. The most challenging aspects of working with the child. 26. During the debriefing in the classroom, participants discuss and summarize the following skills: Approaching a sick child. Gaining the child’s attention. Following the child’s lead by focusing on their interests rather than distracting them. Playing and communicating with the child. Encouraging the child to increase their activity level and develop new skills. Praising the child. 27. Discuss which activities were appropriate for sick children and the reasons behind their suitability. 28. During outpatient sessions, participants observe a 15-minute demonstration and complete a checklist, which includes: Greeting the caregiver warmly. Observing the interaction between the caregiver and the child, focusing on: How the caregiver demonstrates awareness of the child’s movements. How the caregiver comforts and shows love to the child. How the caregiver corrects the child. Asking questions to understand how the caregiver plays and communicates with the child, such as: How do you play with your child? How do you talk to your child? How do you encourage your child to smile? How do you think your child is learning? Praising the caregiver. Advising the caregiver on play and communication activities to do at home, explaining how these activities will support the child’s growth and learning. Checking the caregiver’s understanding by having them practice the activity with the child and ensuring they can apply it at home. Asking about any problems and helping to resolve them. 29. During the debriefing in the classroom, participants discuss and summarize examples of: Positive interactions where the caregiver was attentive to the child, and the child responded by looking at the caregiver. Negative interactions where there was minimal connection between the caregiver and the child. Other characteristics, such as the child’s activity level, happiness, and responsiveness. Changes in caregiver-child interactions during the activities. Challenges caregivers identified in performing activities at home and what helped them overcome these challenges. 30. Additionally, discuss what participants found easy and what they found difficult.
